Some of the silt load reaching Howard Creek would be deposited on the stream bottom; the remainder would be conducted downstream to Lake Jocassee. The degree of siltation of Howard Creek and Lake Jocassee would be dependent upon weather conditions during construction and the adequacy of the preventive control measures taken (see Subsection 4).
If large amounts of silt and sand were to be deposited on the streambeds, it could be difficult for the stream to transport this material out of the system. Langdon, et al., (1976) reports that sediment transport to an appreciable extent occurs only during fairly high flows. Flows of at least 20-40 cfs at station H7 and 50-70 cfs at station H1 (Figure 2-2) are required for significant transport. They also concluded that fine sediments were quickly flushed from Howard Creek, but that coarse sedimentary material of sizes comprising bed-load could present a problem, requiring higher flows to remove this material from the system. Deposition of coarse sediments could result in covering of cobble areas in Howard Creek and changes in the present physical characteristics of the streambed. Langdon et al. (1976) suggests the possibility of storm flow augmentation to help carry sediments from Howard Creek, thereby hastening recovery (Section 4).
Regardless of the control measures taken (Section 4), the stream habitat and aquatic communities in Howard Creek would be adversely affected by silt-laden runoff from the proposed Bad Creek project during the construction period and for a significant period thereafter. Reductions in the abundance of benthic fauna and destruction of their habitat would result from increased siltation (Boyne and Ingram, 1975). This would accentuate a community shift from forms normally inhabiting rock and cobble bottoms to those associated with sand and silt substrates, with a subsequent decline in overall stream productivity.
Applicant (Exh. S) states that "during construction and for a significant period of recovery, conditions in at least 3.5 miles and 9.2 acres of Howard Creek will be rendered unsuitable for trout habitation from Highway 171 downstream to Lake Jocassee." A reduction in benthic fauna would have an adverse impact on trout using these organisms for food. Substrate alteration and destruction of redds caused by increased turbidity and sedimentation would also have an adverse impact on spawning and egg survival.
